chunks: "A BJT has two PN junctions, base-emitter and base-collector, and the mode is just whether each one is forward or reverse biased. That gives four modes.
Cutoff is both junctions reverse biased, or at least V BE below about 0. 5 volts. No base current, essentially no collector current, so it's an open switch.
Forward-active is base-emitter forward biased and base-collector reverse biased. This is the amplifier mode. V BE is about 0. 7 volts, V CE is above about 0.
3 volts, and the collector current is beta times the base current. Saturation is both junctions forward biased. V CE collapses to about 0. 1 to 0.
3 volts, and the collector current is limited by the external circuit, so it's less than beta times the base current. That's the closed-switch mode.
Reverse-active is base-emitter reverse biased and base-collector forward biased, so the emitter and collector swap roles.
It works, but with a very low gain, so it's rarely used on purpose. To check which one I'm in, I look at the voltages. If V BE is below about 0. 5 volts it's cutoff.
If V BE about 0. 7 volts and V CE 0. 3 volts, it's active. If V BE about 0. 7 volts and V CE about 0. 2 volts, it's saturated.
For a switch I drive well into saturation with a forced beta of about 10, and for an amplifier I bias in the middle of the active region."
